rubrics.criterion: The primary-key-dependent capabilities (creating a new record, locating the key column, exposing an owning-table descriptor, reading the key value, providing a scan target for a newly assigned key, reporting key presence, and assigning a key) are no longer required members of the shared row and relation-descriptor contracts that every relation owner must satisfy; they are reachable through a narrower contract so that only relations with a single-column primary key carry them, under whatever interface names and composition the repair chooses.
rubrics.rationale: This is the central obligation of this instance: the task asks for the record tier to be separated from the general row/relation surface it was folded into, and every other obligation follows from that boundary.

rubrics.criterion: Owners that cannot have a single-column primary key — the fixture view and composite-key models used by the test suite, and the information_schema and sqlite introspection models used by reform-db — no longer carry placeholder implementations of the key-dependent capabilities (children whose bodies only return nil or constants, or are empty), and their exported shape exposes only members with real meaning for their kind of relation.
rubrics.rationale: These owners are where the widened contract visibly forces inert behavior into the repository; a repair that restores the boundary must remove those placeholder implementations across every keyless owner, not just in the interface declaration.

rubrics.criterion: The internal query code that uses key-dependent capabilities — the insert pipeline across all three key-receiving conventions, the bulk-insert path with its all-or-none key presence rule, and the column filtering used by inserts and updates (including rejection of key-column updates) — obtains those capabilities through the segregated record/table design and no longer assumes every row or descriptor supplies them.
rubrics.rationale: The uniform-model change rewrote exactly these internal consumers to read record capabilities off the general row surface; leaving them in that form while the contracts claim segregation would keep the forced dependency in place.

rubrics.criterion: The in-repository model generator now emits, for keyless relations, models whose members carry only the schema/descriptor and row/scan surface with working bodies, while keyed relations keep the record-surface members with primary-key-backed bodies; no relation kind gets emitted members that only return inert defaults.
rubrics.rationale: The generator renders models for every downstream user of the library, so the repair is complete only when freshly generated models follow the restored contract tier instead of restoring it solely in the checked-in files.

rubrics.criterion: Every generated model file checked into the repository — the fixture models the test suite compiles against and the reform-db introspection models — is in exact agreement with the repaired generator, so regenerating the models with the repository's own tool produces no changes to the checked-in files (the up-to-date assertions generated for descriptors keep holding).
rubrics.rationale: A key invariant of this repository is that its generated files and go:generate workflow stay in sync; pulling the contracts apart without regenerating leaves the case internally inconsistent even if it compiles.

rubrics.criterion: The exported record and table identifier names in the core package still name a usable contract that keyed relations satisfy (so model files already written by downstream users against those names keep compiling), and the released documentation for those names matches the delivered design.
rubrics.rationale: The task promises compatibility for existing downstream table/record models; a repair that removes or repurposes those names beyond recognition fails that promise even when tests pass.

rubrics.criterion: Members of the shared row and relation contracts are documented uniformly again: no shared member carries qualifiers such as returning nil or doing nothing for some implementing owners, and members documented as never returning an untyped nil keep that meaning for every owner that has them.
rubrics.rationale: The spec'd uniform-model wording survives in interface doc comments; cleaning it up is part of a consistent delivery but does not by itself change the dependency structure of the main judged boundary.

rubrics.criterion: The generator template and the files it renders no longer contain the uniform-model artifacts: no conditional or inline text produces record-surface members with inert default bodies (nil, zero, constant false, empty) or their speculative view wording for keyless relations.
rubrics.rationale: The generator's uniform-model branches produced the placeholder bodies found across the checked-in and all future models; leaving those branches in place would recreate the problem for every newly generated view model.

rubrics.criterion: The not-yet-released section of the project changelog no longer presents the uniform record model nor a blanket regenerate-models instruction tied to it; it describes the record/table tiering actually delivered by the repair.
rubrics.rationale: The changelog entry is the release-facing artifact of the uniform-model work; keeping it after the repair contradicts the delivered design and misleads downstream readers preparing for the same release.

rubrics.criterion: Insert behavior for keyed relations is preserved: an unset key is still cut from column lists where it should be, and the database-assigned key is still written back into the stored row identically under the LastInsertId, OUTPUT INSERTED and RETURNING conventions.
rubrics.rationale: The rewritten insert internals are the paths where a contract-tiering repair is most likely to silently alter SQL or lose the write-back; this pins the concrete observable outcome the suite covers.

rubrics.criterion: Column filtering and bulk behavior for keyed relations is preserved: explicit attempts to update the key column are still rejected with the same rule, and bulk inserts of keyed relations with mixed key presence still fail with the same all-or-none error rather than being reordered, truncated, or accepted.
rubrics.rationale: These guards live in the two helper paths the repair must touch anyway, so a plausible repair can easily reorder the checks or drop one of the guard arms; this criterion pins both sides of the boundary.

rubrics.criterion: A row of a keyless relation is not silently accepted by the record-requiring update, save and delete paths of the core querier: the delivered design either excludes such rows statically through the segregated contract or handles them explicitly, instead of letting them compile through the widened parameter surface, as during the uniform-model experiment, and then reach a nil dereference or silently wrong behavior at runtime.
rubrics.rationale: The widened parameter surface was a direct consequence of the uniform model; an incomplete or careless reform here reintroduces the type hole that the previous boundary prevented.

rubrics.criterion: The reform-db schema-reading flows keep working: models for the information_schema relations and the sqlite introspection relations still scan their rows correctly when querying database metadata, without dropped columns, wrong scan targets, or newly panicked paths introduced by the model rework.
rubrics.rationale: These introspection models are pure view relations regenerated by the repair, and the metadata loading step of the recorded test flow exercises them; the criterion names their concrete regression risk.

rubrics.criterion: The final repository does not mix both designs: for example, the deprecated record/table names do not still alias the widened general contracts while the rest of the code narrows key use to records, and no half-migrated call site keeps reading the key capabilities universally off the shared row surface.
rubrics.rationale: An otherwise sound segregation can be undermined by leftover aliases or a few unconverted consumer sites, which produces the mixed-message design reviewers rejected; it is specific to this instance rather than a generic style issue.
